text:
This research tackles the challenge of text classification, which means sorting and labeling written text. Traditional linear models can struggle to generalize when there are many output classes and very few examples, while complex neural networks can be slow [P2_p1_c04]. 

The main idea behind the tool, called fastText, is a simple text classifier that represents sentences by averaging word information and adding local word order details using groups of adjacent words, known as n-grams [P2_p1_c02][P2_p1_c04][P2_p2_c03]. 

Regarding cost and speed, the research shows that fastText is many orders of magnitude faster for training and evaluation than deep learning classifiers [P2_p1_c02]. It can be trained on more than one billion words in less than ten minutes using a standard multicore computer processor [P2_p1_c02]. Furthermore, it can classify half a million sentences among 312K classes in less than a minute [P2_p1_c02]. 

In terms of accuracy, experiments show that fastText is often on par with deep learning classifiers [P2_p1_c02]. For sentiment analysis, its accuracy is slightly better than certain character-level convolutional networks, and a bit worse than others [P2_p3_c02]. Adding bigram information improves performance by 1% to 4% [P2_p3_c02]. 

As for limitations, the paper notes that unlike some other methods, fastText does not use pre-trained word embeddings, which can explain a 1% difference in accuracy on certain tasks [P2_p3_c02]. The sources do not provide further details on limitations.
